title: The home
description: The dwelling, how it is arranged and kept.
html:
Read in the Ide dialect. The original is written in Igbo; here the one term that changes is chi → si, Ide has chi: it is the word, and si / sị is how it is widely said. Nothing here is rewritten — the documents stand as written.

The home and the compound — Ụnọ

What a dwelling is, how it is arranged and kept, who shares it, what is honoured in it, and what the household does not carry into it.

Odiana is a revival, and it says so: the the old order order was abolished by force in 1911. The religion's own memorial of it is Obibi 31, and canon.md carries it. So this is not a code handed down unbroken. It is the household's share of a religion being rebuilt, and where the household code adds a rule rather than recovering one, this document says which — as every document in this project does.

And the first claim Odiana makes about a house is not about arrangement. A house is judged as the Ndose is judged: by how it is kept, and by who is fed in it. purity.md is this document's closest sibling and its larger half; what is said there of the temple's ground is said here again of the ground a family lives on, because the religion does not hold two standards of clean.

1 · What the home is, and what it is not

The home is a dwelling, and it is not a temple. It is where a lineage sleeps, eats, works, quarrels, recovers and receives — and the religion does not ask it to be more than that.

| | the home | the Ndose | |---|---|---| | what it is | a dwelling, and a compound shared with neighbours | the assembly's ground, and a parish | | who keeps it | the household, by its own hand | everyone who uses it, in turn — purity.md §4 | | the household's place | Obi Chi — one place, the household's own | the ancestral place, the altar, the inner room | | the offering | kola, nzu, mmanya, water, at the household's own place | the Igo Ofo service, by a licensed priest | | the ancestors | named aloud by the household, morning and evening, and at the full moon | named aloud with the assembly, at the full moon | | the cleansing of an alu | never by the household | by a licensed priest, with the community present — purity.md §8 | | what may not be in it | emblems that belong to the Ndose | anything not used in the religion |

  • The household keeps one place of its own: Obi Chi — the altar of the personal spirit, "a dedicated space for communicating with one's chi… which can be as simple as an altar" — temple.md §2, doctrine.md §4. It is not a second Ndose, and it is not a shrine.
  • A home is not a shrine, and a household that turns its front room into one has taken the assembly's ground into a private house.
  • The Ndose is where a matter becomes public — the confession, the assembly, the restitution, the festival. A house settles what it can; it does not hold what belongs to the assembly.
  • And the naming, once. The author's source calls the shared courtyard both Ọbịa and obu. In Odiana Obu is the home of the priests (LANGUAGE.md §3). So the courtyard is Ọbịa, and Obu is never used for a room in a house.
  • The compound is the smallest unit of the religion after the person. Not the house, and not the family alone: the compound — the houses, the courtyard, the path, the water and the wall between them, and the neighbours on the other side of it.

2 · The four elements, and the balance of a space

The tradition holds four elements, and a house holds all four. Mmili water, Ọkụ fire, Ana earth, Ikuku air — "not just physical substances but also spiritual forces".

A naming note, made once. The author's source prints the earth both ways — Ana in some chapters and Ana in others. Odiana's form is Ana (LANGUAGE.md §2; doctrine.md §3), and the old form Ana/Ani is kept only inside the the old order names, which is why the earth priest is the eze ana. This document writes Ana.

| element | is | and how the home holds it | |---|---|---| | Mmili, water | life, purification, and the water of the house | fresh water, set each day and emptied each day — at the door and at the Obi Chi; never standing water, anywhere — §7 | | Ọkụ, fire | warmth, transformation, and the life of the hearth | the hearth, and the lamps; a fire lit in a place made for it, kept clean, and never left where it can foul the ground or reach the thatch — §8 | | Ana, earth | stability, grounding, and the ground the house stands on | clay, wood, stone and the packed floor; the planted ground of the compound — §10 | | Ikuku, air | the breath, and communication | windows and vents opened daily, the door and windows set to the wind, the smoke of the hearth and of the herbs carried out — §8 |

And the rule of balance is the source's own: "if your home feels too stagnant (excess Earth), introduce more Air" — a space holds all four, and where one is in excess the others are raised to answer it. The Ndose is ruled the same way (temple.md §4). A room that is shut, dark and heavy is not holier than one that is open.

And Odiana's own caution about the four: they are the four things a house is made of and kept with — not four forces to be adjusted for an outcome. The house is not tuned. It is built, watered, lit, aired, swept and lived in.

3 · chi, and the person in the house

chi is one to a person — the person's own spirit, a fragment of the supreme light, not a god and not a fluid (doctrine.md §4).

The relation is attested, and it is short: onye kwe chi ya ekwe — when a person agrees, their chi agrees. The home's part in that is not mechanical. It is that a person can find, in their own house, the quiet and the order to agree — and that is what every rule in this document is finally for.

  • The place. A small vessel of water on the household's own place is, in the tradition, a complete chi altar — the chi cult is a women's cult in the tradition, and a woman's altar is a small water-filled vessel (doctrine.md §4). Nothing more is needed, and nothing more is owed.
  • The day. The morning begins at first light, facing east, with the offering — §6 step 7.
  • The correction. The source says to "Keep your space clean and organised to allow your Chi to flow freely." Odiana does not say a chi flows, and a house is not a channel. The space is kept clean and ordered so that the person living in it can be clear enough to agree — which is the whole of the doctrine and none of the metaphor.
  • And the space does not deliver a destiny. The tradition's own limit stands: a diviner may do great things, "but when it comes to one's destiny… you are the only one that can save yourself." A person who arranges a room well and does nothing else has arranged a room.
  • The three enemies are the ones the tradition names — greed, pride and fear — and a house can hold all three. No arrangement removes them. What the home can do is what Ọra and the law do: the shared meal, the ordered house, the debt settled, the quarrel carried to the right place — §11.

4 · What Odiana does not say

The author's source is a modern book of design, and it says many things in a modern register. Odiana keeps the practices and refuses the vocabulary — LANGUAGE.md §1: no New Age or Western occult vocabulary, and no private register of any other project.

| the source says | Odiana says | |---|---| | "positive energy", "energy flow", "attract positive energy" | the state of the place, named plainly — clean or not clean, light or dark, air moving or still, in repair or out of it. What moves through a house is air, water, light and people | | "Similar to Feng Shui", "Just as in Feng Shui" | the rule is kept, and the comparison is dropped — §5. Feng Shui's apparatus is not carried, and its name is not used | | "sacred geometry" | the circle, and the forms the tradition actually uses — §5 | | "smudging" | burning ogilisi or uziza — the tradition's own herb and the tradition's own act | | "prosperity", "abundance" | the law, not the attraction. Poverty is alu in this religion (doctrine.md §8). A bowl of water does not produce wealth, and Odiana does not teach that anything in a room does | | "affirmation", "intentions", "resonates with" | the offering and the naming. A word said in this religion is said to someone | | "wellness", "holistic", "sanctuary", "spiritually charged" | the quiet part of the house, and the healing house beside the Ndose | | "the universe" as an agency | Chukwu, Ana and the alusi — and no name is carried into an Igbo word | | the case studies — a named professional, a family, a firm, a wellness centre | a rule. The religion does not keep testimonials as doctrine | | the recommended reading, which includes another African tradition's cosmology | the sources named in canon.md, and nothing else | | Nye kwe, Chi ya ekwe | onye kwe chi ya ekwe — the attested form (doctrine.md §4) | | the ancestors printed Ndi Ichie | ndị ichie — the form Odiana writes |

And the correction this document makes to its own source, once and plainly: the supreme being is Chukwu. The source names the supreme being in more than one way. Odiana uses one name, and it is Chukwu — the old order and Central Igbo both (LANGUAGE.md §2) — and it uses no other.

And the deities are the alusi — a class of their own below Chukwu (doctrine.md §2) — called alusi, and by no other word.

5 · Ọnọdụ Ọchịchị — the commanding position, and the arrangement of a room

The rule, in one line: a person sits, sleeps, cooks and works where they can see the way in, and are not in line with it.

| where | the rule | |---|---| | the bed | see the door, never in line with it; the head to a solid wall, not under a window, and not with the feet to the door | | the seat | the principal seat of a room faces the way in, with a wall behind it — "the space behind you is solid and supportive" | | the workspace | the desk faces the door; a person does not work with their back to an open way | | the hearth | "Place the stove so that you can see the entrance to the kitchen while cooking" | | the Obi Chi | chosen once, in a place the household can come to without turning its back on the house |

And what the rule is not. The commanding position is the author's own teaching, kept here and marked as kept — the Igbo corpus this project holds does not carry it, and the source itself introduces it by comparing it to Feng Shui. Odiana keeps the seating and not the system, and it does not claim the rule is ancient.

And the second half of the rule, which the source states and the religion holds: "it's about creating a mindset of control and awareness" — the arrangement is a rehearsal. A person who arranges a room so as to be aware of who comes in is practising being aware.

The arrangement

  • The circle above all. "Arrange furniture in a circular or semi-circular fashion to promote unity and flow." A shared room is arranged in a circle or a half-circle, and the seating faces itself rather than a wall or a screen.
  • Sharp corners are not put where people sit, and nothing is set at a height where a head passes under it.
  • Paths are kept clear — from the door to the seats, from the seats to the hearth, and through the compound. Nothing is left standing in a path, not even for a day.
  • The round forms are the tradition's own — round rugs, round baskets, round pots, round stools — and they are used because they are made, not because a shape has power.
  • A naming note. The source calls the circle Okike. In the old order, Okike is the creation — "Okike — the Creation aspect of Chukwu" (doctrine.md §1). Odiana does not use Okike for the arrangement of a room. It keeps the word the source itself gives for a circle — Okilikili — and leaves Okike to the creation it belongs to.
  • The triangle, which the source names Nkọlọ, is kept where the religion already keeps it — at the altar and the standing emblems (temple.md §4). It is not required of a room.
  • And the source's spiral, and its name, are not carried. This project's corpus does not attest them, and Odiana does not adopt a word it cannot source.
  • The compound is arranged around its courtyard, which the source calls Ọbịa — §11.
  • And a room is not filled. A room holds the work done in it; what is not for that work is not in it — §6.

6 · Ịdị Ọcha — the keeping of the house and the compound

Cleanliness is doctrine, and this is the firmest rule in the religion. It is stated first at the Ndose (purity.md), and it is stated here because most members of Odiana will keep it in a house and a compound, every day, for the whole of their lives.

And the doctrine of it is the same doctrine: "When someone commits nso, it affects the whole community." So a dirty place is not a private failing — it is everybody's. A compound is not a row of private houses; it is one ground with several doors on it.

And the three states, in household terms:

| state | in a house | |---|---| | ọcha | clean, white, clear, in good order — the ordinary and required state of the compound, the house, the vessels and the clothes | | nso | set apart: the Obi Chi is not a shelf, the offering plate is not a plate, and the names of the ancestors are not said idly | | alu | the house of an abomination — and the household does not cleanse it. ikpu alu is licensed, through the eze ana (purity.md §8) |

The daily keeping of a house

| # | what is done | why | |---|---|---| | 1 | the ground is swept — with a palm broom, at dawn, before anything else: the house, the courtyard, the path to the door | sweeping is the religion's first act, and it is a rite: "the sweeping away of unwanted influences and the restoration of spiritual purity" | | 2 | the sweepings are carried away and burned or buried | sweepings left at the wall or behind the house have not been removed | | 3 | the surfaces are wiped with clean water — the sill, the stools, the table, the hearth, the Obi Chi, the vessels | | | 4 | the water is emptied and filled fresh — every vessel | standing water is not clean water | | 5 | the yard is raked or smoothed, and the drain cleared | the compound's ground is an orderly surface, not a swept one | | 6 | the threshold is washed | the boundary between outside and inside is washed daily, and it is the part of the house washed most | | 7 | the morning sun is taken — Anyanwu Ututu, facing east, before ten | "the best form of spiritual hygiene and the greatest instrument for conducting morning rituals" | | 8 | the offering is made at the Obi Chi — kola, water, and a libation | §13 |

At dusk: the offering again, the water emptied and refilled, and the house and compound walked once — the doors, the hearth, the wall, the yard — to see that nothing has been left.

And the sweeping is not delegated. purity.md §4 will not let the Eze keep a servant to sweep the Ndose. The same rule holds at home: the head of the household sweeps, the newest member sweeps, and a guest who is staying sweeps. A religion whose cleanliness is doctrine cannot delegate it.

Decluttering, and what it is for

  • Clutter is not a blockage of a flow. It is the other half of dirt — things that are not used, not in repair, and not for anybody.
  • The test of the hand. The source asks the householder to decide whether each object is water, fire, earth or air, and to remove it if it aligns with none. Odiana does not ask that — a chair belongs to sitting — and it asks four plain questions instead: does this belong to a work done in this house? is it used? is it in repair? is it for someone else? A thing that fails all four goes out.
  • And what goes out goes to a person — to a household that needs it, or to be sold, or, if it is waste, to be burned or buried as the sweepings are. Nothing is moved to the back of the house to grow old there.
  • Nothing is stored against a wall, in a path, on a step, or over a bed.
  • The store is a room, not a heap.
  • Under the bed is empty. The source's own rule: "Keep the bedroom free of clutter, especially under the bed."
  • And the work of decluttering is done in the open, not in shame. A household does not hide its things from its neighbours; it gives them away in front of them.

The threshold, and the person

  • Hands washed and mouth rinsed before the offering, at the door — the household's small washing place is the same act as the temple's, and it is the Shinto inheritance, declared here as it is declared in purity.md §2.
  • Shoes. Barefoot entry is the firmest rule of the Ndose (purity.md §5). At home it is each household's own rule, kept at its own door and not imposed on a guest — because a house receives strangers and children, and the required thing is water for the hands of everyone who comes in to eat.
  • And the purity that is not physical. A person who enters clean and carrying a lie has not entered clean. Anger, deceit and a debt unpaid are defilements in a house as they are in a Ndose, and Nchegharị — the confession — is their cleansing. A household that sweeps daily and owes its neighbour money is not a clean household, and the debt is settled before the quarrel reaches the assembly — §11.

And the shared guilt

A dirty place is not a private failing; it is everybody's. A member who walks past filth on the way to the Ndose has misread the religion (purity.md §9) — and a member who walks past it inside their own compound has misread it twice.

And no household is shamed for poverty. The keeping costs water, a broom, nzu and white cloth, and the religion's law says "No citizen of Odiana may fall into destitution" (purity.md §11). A household that cannot afford what the keeping costs is helped by the compound; it is not fined by it.

7 · Water in the home

Fresh, moving, or emptied. There is no fourth state of water in an Odiana house.

  • The vessels are emptied and filled daily — the drinking water, the vessel at the Obi Chi, the bowl at the door. Emptying is the rule; a full vessel left standing is not the keeping.
  • The source's bowl is kept and the source's fountain is not. The source says: "add a small indoor fountain or place a bowl of clean water in the eastern part of your home." The bowl is kept: set clean, facing the east, emptied at dusk. The fountain is not kept where it holds still water, because no standing water is allowed anywhere in the religion's ground (purity.md §6), and a decorative pool indoors is standing water with a name.
  • Outdoors, water is given a channel, a run, or a drain. A pond is kept moving or emptied and cleaned, and never left where mosquitoes breed and children drink.
  • Water is not fouled. "Nothing used pollutes land or water." No soap, no ash, no refuse and no waste is put where the rain will carry it into a stream, a well, or a neighbour's ground.
  • The drains run clear, and are cleared whenever they do not.
  • The roof's run is led away — from the wall, and away from the neighbour's ground.
  • A vessel that holds drinking water is covered, because the code's business is the water people drink.

8 · Light and air — Ọkụ na Ikuku

The rule in one line: no room of an Odiana house is kept dark and still.

| | the keeping | |---|---| | the light | curtains, shutters and doors are opened daily, at waking — the eastern rooms first, because the sun comes there first. Anyanwu Ututu is taken facing east, before ten — purity.md §4 | | the lamp | a lamp at the Obi Chi, and a light at the threshold — the source's candle is kept as what it is here: ọkụ, a fire in a place made for it, never left burning where thatch or cloth can reach it | | the daylight | a room whose work is done by daylight is worked by daylight. Work that can be done before dark is not left for a lamp | | the air | windows and vents opened daily in every room, and the door and windows set to catch the wind. The air of the house is changed each day as the water is | | the smoke | the smoke of cooking and the smoke of the herbs is carried out, not left to sit — and nothing is burned in a room where people sleep | | the scent | the smoke that cleanses in this religion is ogilisi or uziza (purity.md §2) — not an imported incense, and not a perfume worn by a person | | the devices | fans, vents, screens and purifiers are tools, not rites. The requirement is air that moves; how it is moved is the builder's business | | the mirror | for light, and never as a device. A mirror is hung where it carries the sun into a dark corner. It is not hung to turn anything away — that is Feng Shui's business, and §4 | | the dark corner | a corner that cannot be lit is opened — a window, a vent, a lighter wall — or it is not used for anything that matters. Light walls and light surfaces are kept, as the source says |

And the reason, in the religion's own terms rather than the source's: light is Anyanwu, the witness of truth (doctrine.md §7), and air is the breath. A room that keeps neither is a room where a person cannot be seen clearly and cannot breathe well — and it is also, plainly, a room that smells, mildews and sickens, which is what the healing house at the Ndose is for.

9 · Symbols and colours

The religion's colours are three, and they are the temple's (temple.md §4).

| mark | is | where it is used in a home | |---|---|---| | white — ọcha | purity, and peace | akwa ọcha, white cloth: at the Obi Chi, on the table of an offering, and for the dead. The rooms kept for prayer and quiet | | red — ufie | life, and the vitality of the house | in small measure — a binding, a dye, a cloth. "Use red in moderation", and it is never a whole room | | green — ndụ | growth, and the living things of the compound | the planted ground, and the plants in the rooms. A plant in a house is a green kept well or a green dying, and a dying plant is not a decoration | | nzu | purity, and the mark of a threshold | at the threshold, the doorposts, the Obi Chi and the boundary of the compound — renewed whenever it is washed or worn | | ofo | authority, and truth, from the ancestors | held, and kept by the lineage. It is not hung over a door and not set out as a decoration. Where a lineage holds an ofo it stands at the household's own place of authority, as it stands at the inner room of the Ndose (temple.md §9) | | ikenga | personal force, and achievement | at the seat of the one who keeps the ground (temple.md §9) — and never activated with blood | | okpesi | the source's own word for the carved ancestral figures | kept, where a lineage keeps them, at the lineage's own place — which this project has left unnamed (decisions.tsv, D16). The household does not coin a name for it | | blue, and black | the source gives them for water | not the religion's marks. Blue and black in a room are a household's own taste, and not a rule of Odiana | | ọgwụ | the source calls it a protective charm | the charm is not carried — §12. In its other sense ọgwụ is medicine, and medicine is kept |

And one rule is over all of them: in this religion a symbol is not a device. A mark of Odiana says what is already the case; it does not cause what is not. nzu at the door says the threshold is kept — it does not make it kept, and it does not keep anything out by itself. A household that marks its door and does not sweep it has hung a symbol over a mess.

10 · Respect for the land — Ana

The ground under a house is Ana's as much as the ground under a temple (doctrine.md §3), and the household is answerable for it in the same way.

  • Build around it. "Avoid disrupting natural features like trees, rocks, or water sources." A tree is not removed for a view, and the house is set where the ground allows rather than the ground being levelled for the house.
  • And where the ground must be broken, the ground is asked — with kola, nzu and a libation, before building, digging or felling, as at the siting of an Ndose (temple.md §3): "perform rituals to seek permission from the land spirits before building." The household asks for itself; it does not need a priest to ask.
  • What is put in the ground returns to the ground. Nothing is buried in the compound that will not return to the soil — no plastic, no metal, no cement — and this is the tradition's own burial rule turned on everything a household puts down.
  • Nothing fouls water — §7. The refuse pit is set away from the well, the stream and the wall, and it is covered.
  • The waste of the household is dealt with and not left: refuse in its pit, sweepings burned or buried, and nothing at the edge of the compound to be dealt with later.
  • Planted ground is kept planted, and bare ground is kept smooth.
  • The compound's edge is kept as the compound. purity.md §6 says dirt on the road to the temple is dirt at the temple. So: the path in front of the compound, the drain beside it, the wall and the land under the wall.
  • And a member cleans what is in front of them — not as a duty assigned, but because the religion's first act is sweeping (purity.md §9).

11 · Ọra — the compound as a shared place, and the duty to the neighbour

Ọra is community, and the source's own gloss is "collective responsibility". The home is where it is practised or not practised, and the compound is the smallest place it can be practised in.

  • The compound has a shared middle. The courtyard — Ọbịa — is where the household eats, where work is done together, and where a visitor is received: "a central courtyard … the heart of the home".
  • The shared things are kept by all who use them — the path, the well or the tap, the drain, the wall, the roof's run, the tree that gives the shade. A person who uses a shared thing and never mends it is living on the neighbour.
  • The compound eats together. "Share meals with family and friends to foster community and togetherness." And no household of Odiana eats behind a shut door while a neighbour's children go hungry. The law says no citizen of Odiana may fall into destitution (purity.md §11) — and hunger next door is the compound's business before it is the assembly's.
  • A visitor is fed, and the threshold is clean for them. "A clean entrance … shows respect for visitors and ancestors" (purity.md §5).
  • A household keeps its smoke off the neighbour's roof, its waste out of their water, its animals out of their ground, and its quarrels out of the night.
  • The boundary is agreed and marked. Between compounds, as between a temple and the ground around it: marked with nzu or with planted herbs, and moved only by agreement — the law holds that moving a sacred boundary stone is an offence, and the stone is returned and the wound sealed (doctrine.md §8).
  • And the wrong between neighbours is settled low and early. The remedies are the law's own: theft — restitution fourfold; injury — not retaliation, but the offender works the victim's farm for a full planting season; a false oath — banishment until public confession (doctrine.md §8). The assembly is the last place a dispute should be carried, and a household that carries every quarrel there has not kept Ọra.
  • And the guilt is shared. "When someone commits nso, it affects the whole community." One dirty house in a compound is the compound's dirt — §6.

12 · Protection of the home — Ajọ Mmụọ

The source names three means: "Hanging ọgwụ (protective charms) at entrances", "Using nzu (white chalk) to mark thresholds or sacred spaces", and "Planting protective herbs like ogilisi or uziza near the home." Odiana keeps two of the three, and the third by another means.

| kept | how | |---|---| | nzu | at the threshold, the doorposts, the Obi Chi, and the compound boundary — renewed whenever it is washed or worn | | the herbs planted | ogilisi and uziza planted at the edge of the compound and beside the door — planted herbs mark a boundary in the tradition's own practice (purity.md §2) | | the herbs burned | the smoke carried through the house, entrance first: the source says "moving clockwise from the entrance", and Odiana keeps the order — the door, then the rooms, then the compound | | the ground swept, the path clear | the religion's protection is mostly this: a swept ground, a clear drain, a sound door, a repaired wall, a light at the door | | the name said aloud | the guardian of the compound named aloud by the household, as the Ndose names its guardian at consecration and again at Igu Aro (temple.md §9) — "and nothing else is invoked to guard it" | | the boundary sealed with the oblation | where a boundary is repaired or a ground is taken, it is sealed with kola, nzu and mmanya — canon.md A2 |

| not kept | why | |---|---| | the charm hung at the door — ọgwụ | no charm, no bundle, no buried object and no blood-marking is used in this religion (temple.md §9) | | a thing buried at the threshold, under the floor, or in the foundation | the same rule | | a thing killed at the door, the boundary or a new house | an animal is killed at the boundary, in the open, and its blood is spilled on open ground away from the shrine — the tradition's own rule for it is "white animals, such as rams or chickens", and the religion keeps the animal. And what is brought to the shrine itself is the oblation: kola (oji), white chalk (nzu), palm wine (mmanya) and water, for no blood is brought to a shrine in this religion. This is an amendment, enacted as iwu, dated and published, and registered in canon.md (A11) — a declared modernisation, and not a recovered old custom | | fear kept in the house as a protection | fear is one of the three enemies of the chi, with greed and pride (doctrine.md §4). A house hung about with protections is a house that has not been kept |

And the last word of this section is the first: the protection of a home in Odiana is the keeping of it. nzu, the swept ground, the clear drain, the planted herb and the name said aloud are what a kept house has, and there is no fourth means.

13 · The ancestral place in the home — Obi Chi, and the ndị ichie

The household keeps one place, and it is Obi Chi.

| the rule | | |---|---| | chosen once, and quiet | "a quiet, respectful area in your home", "a place where you can pray and reflect without distractions." Beside the door, or beside the noise of the hearth, is not it | | low, and against a wall | the source's own: a wooden stool or a small table as the base. Nothing of the Obi Chi is set above the head of a seated person | | what is in it | the water vessel (emptied and filled daily), the kola plate, the nzu bowl, the white cloth, the lamp, and, where the lineage holds them, the ofo and the ikenga — §9 | | what is offered | kola, nzu, mmanya and water, morning and evening, with a libation poured on the ground — liturgy.md | | no blood is brought there, and no animal is killed at the household shrine | below | | the ancestors are named aloud | at the offering, and at the full moon with the assembly's thanksgiving (temple.md §9; doctrine.md §5) — "as ancestors are believed to visit and bless the living" | | photographs | the sources give Odiana no rule, and none is invented. A household may keep them or not; they are neither required nor forbidden | | the place is not a shelf | what stands there is what belongs there. Nothing else is laid on it, and nothing is stored under it |

And the household's offering is bloodless, without exception.

The tradition puts animals at a shrine, and it activated sacred objects with blood — ikenga above all. Odiana has replaced the animal with the oblation: kola (oji), white chalk (nzu), palm wine (mmanya) and water. This is an amendment, enacted as iwu, dated and published, and registered in canon.md (A3, A4 and A6) — a declared reform, and not a recovered custom. The household is where it is seen most often, and where it costs the most to keep.

And the warrant is the tradition's own, not a subtraction made here: the tradition never offered blood to the supreme being — "The type of offering made to Chukwu is one made up of kola nut, white chalk and libations of palm and raffia wine" — and its own cult of the dead records "no sacrifice made" to the skulls it venerates (doctrine.md §5). So the bloodless household offering is a form the tradition already takes, and the reform is that Odiana takes it everywhere.

The dead of the household:

  • the body is washed with clean water and wrapped in white, and the grave faces east (doctrine.md §6);
  • the household keeps its own ground clean in the days of the death, and the bereaved do not enter the Ndose until the cleansing the priest sets is done (purity.md §10, §11);
  • and the lineage's place of keeping — where its remains and emblems are held — remains unnamed in this project (decisions.tsv, D16). The household does not coin a name for it.

And a new house is entered with the temple's own six bloodless parts — white cloth, clean water, nzu, kola, the prayer, the libation (temple.md §5). This is Odiana's own application, and it is marked as such: the source gives no consecration for a dwelling, and this document does not pretend one was inherited.

14 · The room-by-room guide

The threshold, and the entrance

  • the door is swept and the threshold washed, daily — the part of the house washed most;
  • nothing is left at the door: no shoes piled in the way, no rubbish, no broken thing, no standing water;
  • the way in is lit — "Light symbolises clarity" — a light at the door, and the door itself kept in repair;
  • nzu marks the threshold and the doorposts, and ogilisi or uziza stands planted beside the door — §12;
  • the entrance is where the household takes the world's dirt, so there is a mat, a place for the shoes, and water for the hands of anyone who comes in to eat;
  • and nothing is hung over the door. No charm, no bundle, and no mark that is not nzu or a plant.

The compound, and the ground outside the wall

  • swept at dawn — the yard, the path to the door, and the path past the neighbour's door;
  • the drain cleared, the wall repaired, the refuse pit covered and set away from the water — §7, §10;
  • the planted ground kept planted: the shade tree, the ogilisi, the uziza, the kitchen garden;
  • the courtyard Ọbịa is the compound's middle, and the care of it is shared — §11;
  • no animal is killed in the compound, and none is kept where it fouls a path, a neighbour or the water — the animal of a festival is killed in the open, beyond the compound;
  • and nothing is thrown over the wall into the neighbour's ground. The edge of the compound is where a household's manners are visible.

The Ọbịa, and the living room

  • seating in a circle or a half-circle — "to promote unity and conversation";
  • the principal seat in the commanding position — §5: facing the way in, with a wall behind;
  • warm and earthy colours, and the religion's three colours used as marks and not as paint — §9;
  • the tradition's own things, and they are used: woven baskets, clay pots, wooden stools, carved work. A room is not a museum of the heritage, and an artefact that is never handled is clutter with a story;
  • the Obi Chi may stand in a quiet part of this room where the house has no separate place — the source allows it: "If space allows, create a small ancestral shrine in a quiet corner of the living room." It is not put where people pass constantly, and not where the noise is;
  • and the shared room is shared: it holds the gathering, the meal and the telling.

The bedroom

  • the bed in the commanding position — see the door, never in line with it;
  • a solid headboard, of wood, "to provide stability and grounding"; the head to a wall, not under a window;
  • kept dark to sleep and opened to wake — aired and lit daily, §8;
  • calm colours — white and the light earth colours, and red kept out of it;
  • nothing under the bed, and nothing stored over the head — §6;
  • the personal marks. The source places the ikenga and the ofo near the bed. Odiana does not put the ofo in a bedroom — an ofo is a lineage's authority and it stands where the household's authority stands, §9 — and the ikenga stands at the seat of the one who keeps the ground (temple.md §9), which is not a bed;
  • and the room is for rest, for illness and for the marriage. Work that can be done elsewhere is done elsewhere.

The kitchen

  • the hearth in the commanding position — "Place the stove so that you can see the entrance to the kitchen while cooking";
  • the food is Ana's and Chukwu's. The source's own words are "Food is a gift from Ana (the Earth) and Chukwu (the Supreme Being)" — and Odiana writes Ana (§2). So the meal is prepared with the offering said and not in a hurry;
  • the fire is kept clean and in repair, and the smoke is carried out — §8;
  • the hearth is never left burning where it can foul the ground or reach the thatch — the temple's own rule for fire (temple.md §4);
  • the kitchen is the room most easily fouled, and therefore the room swept most: after every cooking, and the surfaces wiped with clean water;
  • drinking water is kept covered, and the vessels emptied and filled — §7;
  • clay pots and wooden spoons — the source's own list, and the tradition's: Ana in the kitchen;
  • and the meal is shared — §11. A household that cooks and eats alone, in a compound full of people, has done half of what a kitchen is for.

The store, and where things are kept

  • a store is a room, not a heap, and what is in it is what will be used — §6;
  • grain, yam and seed are laid where damp and rats cannot reach them, and the store is swept and its door shut;
  • tools are mended and put in the place made for them, and a broken thing is repaired or given away, never stacked;
  • nothing is kept against a wall, in a path or on a step — §5, §6.

The Obi Chi

  • the place, the items and the offering are §13, and nothing is added to them;
  • it is kept daily: the water emptied and filled, the surface wiped, the nzu renewed when it wears;
  • it is not a shelf, and nothing is set down on it in passing;
  • the lamp is lit at the offering, and never left burning unattended;
  • and it is the one place in the house that is not rearranged. A household moves its furniture; it does not move the Obi Chi about.

The quiet part of the house

  • one part of the house is kept quiet — the source's own: "Designate a quiet area in your home for healing rituals."
  • it is where a person who is ill lies, and where a person sits when there is something to settle in themselves;
  • nothing is done in it that is not aimed at the cure — the rule of the healing house (temple.md §6) — and no gathering is held in it;
  • it is aired and cleaned daily like every other room, and a sick room is cleaned and not avoided; the household's washing of hands applies here first;
  • and what a house cannot heal is carried to the Ndose — the healer, the diviner and the assembly are there for it (temple.md §6).

And one reform of the source, stated plainly: the household does not compute the moon.

The source tells the household to track the moon's phases and to plan its rearranging, its cleansing and its decluttering by them. In Odiana the calendar is announced, not read locally — the Nzemabua publishes it in Igu Aro, and no Ndose sets its own (doctrine.md §9). So the household keeps the new moon, the full moon and the waning by the announced calendar, and it does not keep its own reckoning and does not settle the year's dates for itself.

And the source's names for the phases are not carried here. This project's corpus does not attest them, and Odiana does not adopt a word it cannot source. The phases are the moon's; the calendar is the religion's.

And the seasons are two as the tradition names them — the rains and the dry. The source names a third, a harvest season. This project's corpus does not carry that name, and it is left to the author rather than adopted.

The blood ruling, in one place

(The ruling is canon.md A11, and it is the same in every document of this religion.)

An animal is killed at every festival of Odiana and at every serious rite of it. The announcing of the year, the cleansing of a great abomination, the taking of a title, the consecration of a Dibia, the setting of a boundary, the burial of a head, the making of peace, and the opening of a war. The animal is killed in the open, and its blood is spilled upon open ground, away from every holy thing.

And no blood is brought to a shrine, or to an altar, or to a sacred object, or to a tree that is held sacred. Nothing holy in this religion is ever touched with blood. The altar keeps the kola, and the nzu, and the wine, and the water. This is a modernisation of Odinana and it is iwu — made, and published, and dated — and it is not a custom recovered from the ancestors.

What remains bloodless, and stays bloodless:

  • the offering to Chukwu — the tradition's own offering was kola, white chalk and libation, and it is kept;
  • the household shrine — the household oblation is kola, nzu, mmanya and water;
  • the temple altar — no blood is brought to it, ever;
  • the consecration of objects — no shrine, Ofo, Ikenga or medicine is made with blood (canon.md A6);
  • a reading of afa — the reading is free: nothing is charged for it, and the offering is not a fee.

And the one blood that is never shed in this religion, in any rite and for any purpose, is human blood. Where the old practice used a human being, this religion uses the fowl — for it is the fowl that is used in performing sacrifice, and not a human being.
